A Messy-cum-Tricky Graph

At first glance, it seems to provide data regarding the amount of time spent readinng a privacy policy and the readibility of text. 
But if I dig deeper, it could not help us actually compare between any two companies' privacy policy. 
For example, if we take two companies on the graph having nearly same reading time ( Netflix and Reddit) and compare them, they have considerable difference in readibility, which suggests that Netlix's would be harder to read than Reddit. So, if reading Netflix's is hard, it should take more time to read than Reddit given the fact that both of them have same reading minutes.

Internet Privacy Policies; excruciatingly long by accident or by design? 

After reading this article, I noticed that the Airbnb privacy policy takes the longest amount of time to read compared to the others, while something like craigslist takes little to none.  It seems companies aren't trying to have their customers read what's laid out for them, hoping people will accept the agreement and turn a blind eye, which makes me wonder if the companies hire people to make these long and grueling terms of service lists on purpose.

This graph is aimed at making average people more aware of how ridiculous these terms and services are in both time and average readability, it shouldn't take a person as long as a movie to read and fully comprehend the terms and service of an app or website before you even use it.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of the surveyed businesses have privacy policies with a readability score above 1300. A reading score of 1300 marks the beginning of the college level complexity range. 

I wonder why the majority of these corporations’ privacy policies are written in a more complex manner that’s more difficult to comprehend from the perspective of a consumer. As a high school consumer of these services, I feel that it is necessary to possess a genuine understanding of my data and how it’s used and distributed. However, due to my current educational background, this understanding I desire is likely much harder for me to grasp in comparison to a college student or professor capable of reading at this level. Ironically, only 33% of Americans over the age of 25 have a college degree that would enable them to do so. It is no secret that there are far less Americans who have graduated college than those who have. So then why would these corporations choose to make their privacy policies so strenuous?

Corporations take advantage of the uneducated public to hide their true intentions “stated” in their privacy policies.

raw_comment: I noticed that the graph depicts the level of difficulty in reading the privacy policies of websites. I’ve noticed that most big corporations use difficult language at a professional level in their policies. I’ve also noticed that most of these companies have policies that take 20-40 minutes to read.  This is because the high reading level makes it difficult for people to understand the policies, so it takes them longer to read. I wonder how they collected this information? Were people asked to read these policies for an experiment, and if so, how many people were taken into account ? I’ve also noticed that the books that were compared to these policies are usually books that are taught in high school. Most of these books are old, so the diction is very difficult, and most people struggle to comprehend these books . However, this graph shows that these texts were easier to read than most of the privacy policies for big companies. So, I think  this graph is attempting to convey the message that big corporations use difficult diction in their policies to scam people into quickly subscribing or using their website/app. Most people will tend to quickly skim over the policies, due to the difficult language, because it’s not likely they would spend 20-40 minutes reading and comprehending this information. These policies could contain loopholes or risks involved in that app that people won’t be able to recognize and may regret later when a problem occurs within the website/app.

raw_comment: This New York Times graph identifies how difficult it is to read an app’s or website’s privacy policies and how long it take to read. What I wonder about this graph is: why there’s books included in the graph, what are the other black unlabeled dots, and how was the readability score measured for each of them? This graph can be used in many ways. For example, this can give teachers ideas to articles that their students can analyze in class depending on if they’re a high school or college student. This graph can also be used for new apps and websites to see how other apps/websites organize their privacy policies. Most of the privacy policy articles are towards the college reading level and above, making their policies harder to read and understand so that more people end up not reading it and accept anyway. Not knowing what they could have just gotten themselves into, which is what companies want.

raw_comment: The graph, at first glance shows the difficulty of reading certain companies privacy policies. As someone who is familiar with certain businesses presented on the graph, I have never read one privacy policy. As consumers, we want to continue on the app, skipping through the “boring” agreements when we first purchase the app. Companies known for presenting news stories are seen towards the middle with the privacy policy taking 15-20 minutes to read. I believe the time taken to read the policy serves importance as it shows what type of companies may take longer to read. Certain social media apps are in the high school and college average lexile reading range, these apps are appealing to consumers. They wouldn’t put their policies in a professional career reading level if teenagers would skim the policy in the first place. I am curious what the dots not emphasized represent, other businesses? I am also curious why a popular app such as airbnb which can be used by anyone would have a such high reading level. Some consumers of the app may have not received high education and wouldn’t know how to comprehend the privacy policy. Businesses should appeal to the consumer. One can infer that companies towards the bottom of the reading level may be used by everyday people, such as “Amazon” or “home depot”. In my opinion, the deeper meaning is companies should appeal to their consumers.

raw_comment: This graph is set up in a way that compares website and app privacy policies’ difficulty and how long they take to read. The first thing I noticed was that many social media pages share similar reading levels, though some take longer to read than others. The next thing I noticed was that larger companies or news sites typically had a much higher readability score than the rest of the graph, yet remained in a medium area for how much time it took to read. There are also popular novels in more faded texts, likely placed to help guide a viewers understanding of the difficulty of each policy. I do wonder what the other smaller dots are meant to represent, although I am guessing that they are smaller name companies or apps. I believe that the deeper story within this graph is to show how the larger companies typically use more confusing or higher level writing, which may confuse or put off the reader from completely analyzing the policies, as shown in larger companies like GoDaddy, Walt Disney, CNN, and CNS Sports. Their reading levels are higher yet time taken to read is low, likely due to readers skimming long privacy policies instead of taking the time to struggle through the more difficult writing. Whether intentional or not, these companies show an odd ratio between difficulty and time taken to read, while social media companies like Snapchat and Reddit maintain a medium difficulty with a medium time taken to read.

I wonder why companies use such inaccessible language in agreements which they expect everyone to read. Are they trying to conceal otherwise unacceptable terms in a shroud of verbosity so that they might slip past the consumer unnoticed? 

“Top Companies Write Nearly Unintelligible Privacy Policies”

raw_comment: Upon opening the graph and examining the data points, I noticed BBC's data point stood out in the crowd. I believe such to be true as BBC’s data point is an outlier in the data set. It takes around 13 minutes to read and has a Lexile score of about 970, which when compared to other apps like Baidu which has a Lexile score of above 1600 and takes 10 minutes to read, makes me wonder what is so different about the terminology and vocabulary used in the privacy policies. I also saw that BBC's data point is different compared to other news station such as CBS Sports and CNN, thus again making me wonder what is so different about the content of the privacy policies that makes the lexile level and time to read higher. I also noticed that political media channels like CNN have a higher Lexile level of around 1600 compared to apps like Vimeo and Snapchat that only have a Lexile level of about 1100 and 1200 respectively. This makes me wonder whether or not the content being displayed and used in CNN is more advanced and requires more outside knowledge than apps like Snapchat and Vimeo do. Overall this graph shows that most social media apps like Reddit, Facebook, and Snapchat that are tailored towards younger audiences have a lower Lexile level and reading time compared to news and media apps like CNN and Airbnb. I would name this graph, "No Wonder We Don't Read These Things."

raw_comment: When I look at this graph, I immediately notice that one of the highest readability privacy policies is for CNN. As displayed on the right side of the graph, CNN is depicted as having a professional career reading level. It also has a somewhat mild reading time. This gives me the idea that higher-level media are more viewed by higher leveled readers due to the fact that it may be more appealing to them. I then look over to things like Snapchat and Reddit and see that they are at a lower reading score. Things like these are commonly seen in use by children and or teens. They also have lower reading times making me think that depending upon the reading material or category of these media, the details in privacy policies change. For example, the app Airbnb has the highest reading time of all data displayed. This may be because of the realm of appeal this app is in is more complex. Airbnb is a system used to book hotel stays. This means that more complex applications like these have more conditional statements for things like policies in a hotel. All of this makes me wonder whether or not developers of these privacy policies pay attention to their target audiences when making them. For example, if social media is targeted towards young audiences, privacy policies should be shorter and at a lower reading level to best appeal to teens. The graph shows higher reading times for these media, however, which is surprising to me. I would name this graph "Privacy Policies: Time to Read?"

raw_comment: I notice that there is a large cluster of website privacy policies that take between about 15 and 25 minutes to read and are at a Lexile reading level of between 1100 and 1600. I find it quite interesting that the graph compares the website policies to reading levels of the first chapters of well-known books. Also, I notice that well-known social media sites such as Snapchat, Vimeo, Reddit, and Yahoo are all at a high school reading level, while Facebook, Netflix, N.Y.T., and Imgur are at a college reading level. This leads me to wonder if there is some correlation between intended 'audiences' for a particular website and how hard they make their privacy policies to understand. This then leads me to further wonder whether websites INTENTIONALLY write more difficult-to-read privacy policies, and if so, for what reason. For example, is Snapchat writing a high-school reading level privacy policy because its creator(s) believe(s) that Snapchat should be used mostly by high schoolers? Are Netflix and Facebook writing privacy policies at college reading levels because their intended audience is people in college or of a general college 'age'? A title for this graph might be, "Uncrackably Cryptic."

I notice that most social media networks like Reddit and Snapchat take about 15 minutes to read the privacy policy and are at the high school reading level. I also notice that most business-related websites like GoDaddy and Eventbrite are at the professional career reading level and take at least 15 minutes to read the privacy policy. In addition, I notice that there are not many websites with readability scores that are under high school reading level, suggesting that many of these apps and websites require this level of reading.

This is because the social media networks’ privacy policy is only at the high school reading level and takes less than 15 minutes to read. I wonder if this is because teenagers are more likely to use these websites than use business-related websites. I also wonder why CNN and BBC have such different reading levels when they both provide similar content.

raw_comment:
1) The graph itself is a visual depiction of an ethical dilemma that puts every user of these websites at risk. On the surface, the graph depicts this notion that privacy policies are often above some users' comprehensible level; however, hidden within this idea is the fact that when users don't understand the conditions, they also cannot defend themselves from them either. 

2) The practice of creating predatory policies that can often circumvent legal protections is not a new concept; however, with more recent privacy crackdowns (such as policy coming from the EU), companies must find ways to maintain their questionable practices while also maintaining an illusion of transparency. YouTube recently came under legal scrutiny for their violations of privacy laws including children. Despite legal protections of children's data, they marketed themselves to advertising companies as a hub for kid-friendly content thus ensuring financial gain. Their defense was centered around their terms of service requiring users to be 13 years or older, yet they don't actually require verification. While they may have been penalized, many instances of predatory data collection fly under the radar.

3) With the rapid development of new technology and data that is readily accessible online, legal diction and confusing verbiage allows companies to take advantage of its consumers from monetary and legal gain. The only way to combat this is to move in the direction of the EU and modernize policy.

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that the Walt Disney Company's privacy policy is difficult to read, even though their content is mainly aimed towards children. Upon doing some research, I found that in 2017, Disney was sued for tracking kid's data through their apps. The only way huge corporation companies, such as Disney, can protect themselves from these types of lawsuits is through their privacy policy. If their privacy policy is complex enough, parents may not take the time to fully understand what they are agreeing to, since they trust that the company always provides safe services for children.
2) I noticed that Netflix and Facebook are right above A Brief History of Time in terms of readability score and Snapchat is below it by 100. The readability score of  A Brief History of Time may be shown on the graph as reaching college level, but I found, more specifically, that the age range is from 15-17. This is important because by 15-17 years old, many teenagers have access to social media and they should be able to understand the privacy policy that is provided with these apps.  
3) I wonder why it took more time to read Etsy's privacy policy rather than the policies for Netflix, Facebook, Snapchat, and Imgur. Was the privacy policy for Etsy actually a lot longer? Considering that the readability score does not change drastically between these companies, it really makes me wonder if people value their money  spent on Etsy and  its return policies, rather than their privacy.
